unsigned char and signed char nodes as integers (#1499)

* Encode unsigned char and signed char nodes as integers

Decoding has treated these two types as integers since #864, and #1459 made
the Emitter write them as integers, but convert<T>::encode still routed them
through the generic inner_encode overload, which streams the raw byte. So
Node(uint8_t{16}) produced the scalar "\x10" and a Dump/Load round trip threw
bad conversion, which is the convert.h half of #1027.

Give unsigned char and signed char their own inner_encode overload, matching
the shape of the existing ConvertStreamTo special case just below it. Plain
char is untouched and still encodes as a single character.

* Pin Emitter output for signed char

std::int8_t has no operator<< overload of its own, so it reaches the int
overload by integral promotion and already emits as a number. That is
correct but accidental: adding a signed char overload that mirrors the
char one would silently turn it back into a quoted character, and #1459
added a test only for the unsigned side.

Verified by adding exactly that overload, at which point the new test
fails with "- \"\x10\"\n- \"\xf9\"" while UnsignedEightBitInteger keeps
passing.

Encode unsigned char and signed char nodes as integers (#1499)

* Encode unsigned char and signed char nodes as integers

Decoding has treated these two types as integers since #864, and #1459 made
the Emitter write them as integers, but convert<T>::encode still routed them
through the generic inner_encode overload, which streams the raw byte. So
Node(uint8_t{16}) produced the scalar "\x10" and a Dump/Load round trip threw
bad conversion, which is the convert.h half of #1027.

Give unsigned char and signed char their own inner_encode overload, matching
the shape of the existing ConvertStreamTo special case just below it. Plain
char is untouched and still encodes as a single character.

* Pin Emitter output for signed char

std::int8_t has no operator<< overload of its own, so it reaches the int
overload by integral promotion and already emits as a number. That is
correct but accidental: adding a signed char overload that mirrors the
char one would silently turn it back into a quoted character, and #1459
added a test only for the unsigned side.

Verified by adding exactly that overload, at which point the new test
fails with "- \"\x10\"\n- \"\xf9\"" while UnsignedEightBitInteger keeps
passing.
